cards.front: What are the five stages of solving a computational problem, in order?
cards.back: **Understand** the problem, **plan** an algorithm, **implement** it as a program, **test** it with a range of inputs, then **evaluate** and refine the result.
cards.hint: Start with what is given and what must be produced.

cards.front: Why is abstraction useful when designing a program?
cards.back: It removes detail the problem does not need, leaving a **model** with only the essential features. A library system stores a book's title and borrower, not its cover colour.
cards.hint: Think of an underground map that leaves out streets.

cards.back: Breaking a large problem into smaller **sub-problems** that can each be solved and tested separately, then combined into the full solution.
cards.hint: Think of a school concert split into tickets, lighting and music.

cards.back: A **finite sequence of unambiguous steps** that solves a problem or completes a task, always leading to a result.
cards.hint: It is the plan you make before writing any code.

cards.back: Identifying **similarities or repeated features** within a problem or between problems, so an approach can be reused.
cards.hint: Sorting names and sorting prices have something in common.

cards.back: Turning a recognised pattern into a **single solution** that works for a whole class of problems, not just one case.
cards.hint: Compare a routine that adds any two numbers with one that adds only 3 and 4.

cards.back: A **named input** to a routine whose value is supplied each time the routine is used, so the repeated steps stay fixed.
cards.hint: Which values change each time the routine runs?

cards.front: A student starts writing code as soon as a problem is given. What is the error?
cards.back: They skip **understanding the problem**. Without a clear plan, mistakes are much harder to find later.

cards.front: Does abstraction mean losing any important detail?
cards.back: No. Abstraction removes only the detail that is **irrelevant** to the purpose, so essential features must stay.

cards.front: When asked for an example of decomposition, what should you do first?
cards.back: Name the **whole problem** first, then list the sub-problems it splits into.

cards.front: Why does spotting a pattern save effort?
cards.back: Once one part is solved, you can **reuse the same approach** on similar parts. Patterns also help predict what a program will do next.
cards.hint: Think about solving one part and applying it elsewhere.

cards.front: Why is a generalised solution more useful than one written for a single case?
cards.back: It uses **parameters** to handle many inputs, avoids rewriting similar code, and one tested solution is easier to maintain.
cards.hint: Count how many copies of the code you would otherwise need.

cards.front: How do pattern recognition and generalisation relate in order?
cards.back: **Pattern recognition** comes first, noticing what repeats. **Generalisation** follows by writing one solution that works for all such cases.
cards.hint: Which one notices, and which one writes the solution?
